I have been farming in Quzhou for over thirty years, and I know this land well. My family has about 5 mu of good irrigated land, and every year I grow winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same plots — that is the rotation that works here on the North China Plain. I sowed the wheat last October before the ground froze, and now that spring has arrived the wheat is greening up and needs care. I will apply a topdressing of urea when the wheat reaches the jointing stage, and I will irrigate three times: once now to help it recover from winter, once at jointing, and once at heading. I also need to spray for weeds and watch out for aphids and rust, so I will make about four pesticide applications in total. I use a rotary tiller to prepare the wheat field because that is what I have always done.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I will immediately plant hybrid maize seed — I buy the "Nongda" varieties from the shop in town because they give good yields. I do not plow for the maize; I plant directly into the wheat stubble to save time and labor, since the summer season is short. For the maize, I will put down compound fertilizer at planting and irrigate twice, once when it is young and once at flowering. I will spray for weeds and corn borers about three times. I do not grow cotton this year because my children are working in the city and I do not have enough hands to manage the extra labor. Wheat and maize are stable crops, and I can sell them easily to the grain buyers who come to the village. I expect the wheat to give me about 500 kg per mu and the maize about 550 kg per mu if the weather cooperates.
